prompt:
A densely annotated editorial infographic plate, drawn by hand in confident ink
line with light watercolour and gouache wash on bright warm-white paper.
Contour line varies in weight and is charcoal near-black. Dimensional but not
photographic: restrained hatching, subtle texture, believable volume, selective
shadow, clean uncluttered background. Every material reads as itself — dull grey
lead, unglazed earthenware, weathered timber, damp fibrous bark — and materials
that differ in the explanation look visibly different. Quiet palette of stone,
clay, wood, and metal tones over the warm-white ground, with one or two
desaturated accents that each keep a single meaning throughout the plate.
Contemporary editorial typography: one calm display face for the title, one
highly legible face for the many small labels, sentence case, crisply printed
and correctly spelled. Annotation is dense and disciplined — leader lines,
brackets, dimension marks, magnified inset circles, small side studies — laid
out so no two leaders cross. Asymmetric composition with about a quarter of the
page left quiet. Modern printing on clean stock: fresh, crisp, and unaged. The
only lettering anywhere on the plate is the title, the deck, the labels, and the
short notes. The words hero, drawing, figure, plate, inset, zone, band, strip,
trio, column, and cutaway describe the construction of the page and are never
lettered onto it, alone or in a phrase: no headings that name parts of the
layout, no percentages or
proportions of the page, no tags in brackets after a label or note, no sentence
describing the drawing or explaining what the reader is meant to see, no
signature, monogram, date, watermark, or credit line.

Title, set largest at the top left of the page: proofscan
Deck beneath it: A lantern-and-clipboard walk through the research shelves — every document's extracted text is glanced at, judged by eye, and no coin is spent.

Hero: a night inspection of a modest archive room. Long shelves recede along the left, each shelf bearing a small brass label — one readable as trades, one as mills, one as glass — and on every shelf the volumes stand in pairs: a bound source document and, tucked against it, its thin typed transcript. An inspector's rolling cart moves along the aisle carrying only a lantern, a clipboard, and a hand lens; a note on the cart: no scholar is consulted and nothing is paid — the checks are quick looks, not readings.

The centre shows three glances the lantern makes, drawn as three small lit vignettes in a vertical band:
- a pair whose transcript is missing entirely, only a dusty gap beside the source, marked with a heavy cross;
- a transcript unrolled to reveal a single curt printed line — this page has not been digitized — marked with the same heavy cross, captioned: placeholder words are a certain failure;
- a transcript peppered with hollow diamond marks among its letters, held under the hand lens, marked with a wavering question, captioned: too many unreadable characters make a text suspect.

At the right, the inspector's finished report pinned to the aisle's end post: a ruled sheet with one row per shelf and three tallied columns headed OK, SUSPECT, FAILED, and beneath the table two short lists of named offenders, each with its reason in small script. A note at the report: the point is aim — the paid, careful proofreader is sent only where this walk found trouble.

One quiet detail at the lower left: a very slim transcript standing beside a thick source volume, a small measuring notch beside it, captioned — a text far too short for its book is suspicious on size alone.

One warm accent colour marks the lantern light and the tally columns; the shelves, volumes, and night stay in ink and grey wash.
